title: Sebastian Quill and the Queen's Crazy Canvas
markdown:
The portrait hall smelled of linseed, turpentine, and the particular patience of expensive light. Tall windows poured afternoon onto the parquet until the floor looked varnished twice. A clock in the next room counted as if it, too, were sitting for a likeness. Sebastian Quill set his easel where the glow would be kind to a chin. He was the royal portraitist. His brushes were not magic, whatever the court pamphlets claimed, but they could catch a knowing eye, a jester’s smirk, and — if the week demanded it — the fluff of Queen Adelina’s seven very particular lapdogs.

He had painted those dogs separately, once, in a quieter month. The sketches still lived in a drawer: Fifi Fluffernutter, teeniest of the lot, diamond collar winking with more sass than a pixie, voice like a complaining bell, certain she was a fairy queen in ethereal light. Bartholomew — Barty Bumblesnout to anyone who had been kissed by him — a happy whirlwind who believed himself a dragon slayer of approximately one billion imaginary beasts, complete with an internal soundtrack of whoosh and roar. Duchess Dainty Paws, poodle of immense dignity and a hairdo that required its own weather, posing as a philosopher while contemplating the nearest biscuit. Sir Reginald Rufflebutt, face like a worn leather armchair, jowls wobbling, demanding a tiny sparkly sword because a knight needed one. Princess Poofington III, a white cloud of elegance, already halfway to angel. Captain Cuddles, scruffy terrier of pantry expeditions, nose for adventure that usually meant biscuit geography. Lord Snugglepants, connoisseur of naps, wishing to radiate Buddha-peace and mostly radiating warmth onto whoever stood still.

Sebastian had survived those sittings. He had not, until today, been asked to put all seven dreams onto one royal face.

Today the commission was the Queen.

“Sebastian, my dear,” Adelina had purred, silk over pebbles, “a portrait that captures my essence. My power. My undeniable magnificence.”

Usually that meant likeness, grace, a regal glow. He had done her once already, years back: fewer jewels, more sleep in the eyes, a sitting in which the dogs had been banished to a velvet rope. That canvas hung in a lesser corridor and was, he suspected, the one she liked. This new request wanted magnificence, which was a different pigment.

Sebastian mixed oils. Linseed on his fingers. The Queen’s face, serene, began to take shape — brow, mouth, the particular patience of someone who had been painted too often. Then the door admitted the first opinion.

Fifi pirouetted. “Master Quill! Fairy wings on a little paw, yes? A halo of moonlight!”

Sebastian’s brush hovered. Wings. On the Queen.

Barty lumbered in, tail thumping. He nudged a wet nose into Sebastian’s shin. “Epic battle. Dramatic fire around the snout.”

Fire. In a state portrait. A bead of sweat found Sebastian’s temple.

Duchess sashayed, tail a sceptre. “Profound contemplation. A scroll. Or a tiny wise owl.” She arranged her brow into biscuit-thought.

Sir Reginald’s jowls wobbled. “Where’s the sword? Don’t paint her like a wilting daisy. A warrior queen.”

Princess Poofington floated, fluff glowing. “Angel wings. Shimmering mist. As if I — she — had just descended.”

Captain Cuddles barked hope. “A map. A compass. Leading us to a very good picnic.”

Lord Snugglepants yawned, stretched, and gave Sebastian a sleepy look that meant lotus, peace, and please do not move the leg he had chosen as a pillow.

The sable brush became Barty’s chew toy; Sebastian rescued it shining with dog. Fifi nosed the palette for glitter and left a paw-print in the crimson, which would later have to be a jewel or a wound. Duchess attempted to abscond with the pearly gouache, convinced it was a new biscuit that had landed by accident; he traded her a real crumb and got the tube back dented. Sir Reginald barked for heroic strokes until the hall’s echo agreed with him. Princess batted sunbeams and, missing, batted a drape into a golden puddle. Captain delivered stray feathers for the exploration map, then a second feather, then a third, as if the Queen might colonise a pillow. Lord Snugglepants snored, a warm heavy kindness against the shin Sebastian envied, and once opened one eye as if to approve a particularly peaceful brushstroke that did not exist.

Then the courtiers, who had heard there was a canvas and therefore a policy. The Prime Minister, pockets jingling, wanted her to hold a miniature treasury, fiscal virtue in gilt. The Head Gardener, soil under every nail, insisted on a once-a-century orchid that was, incidentally, wilting in his own glasshouse; he described the bloom so vividly Sebastian almost painted the wilt. The Royal Historian, spectacles at a crisis, decreed a founding charter the size of a biscuit, every letter legible if you stood on a chair.

Sebastian mixed, wiped, mixed again. He tried, for a quarter of an hour that felt like a reign, to keep the Queen’s true mouth. The mouth kept acquiring other people’s wishes. The canvas ceased to be Adelina and became a carnival that had collided with an art shop. Fairy wings at one shoulder. A dragon scale at the other. A scroll. A sparkly sword. Angel plumage behind the wig. A map unrolling at the feet like a tongue. A golden lotus trying to bloom under a tiny treasury that threatened to tumble into the charter, which threatened to tumble into the orchid, which had already died in another room. His stomach performed unhelpful gymnastics. He wondered, not for the first time, whether integrity was a colour he had forgotten to mix, or merely a quieter room.

The grand doors opened. Queen Adelina glided in, eyes bright, ready for magnificence. Sebastian’s heart changed rhythm. He hid behind the easel and peeked with one eye.

She surveyed the canvas. Silence, thick as varnish. The dogs held their tails still. The courtiers puffed, prepared for any weather.

Then a giggle, bell-like. It grew. It became a laugh that used the whole hall.

“Oh, Sebastian.” She dabbed a tear with lace. “It’s magnificent. It isn’t just me. It’s everything. The aspiration. The joy.”

She pointed at Fifi’s wings — magic for the people — at Barty’s imagined dragon — strength — at the Duchess’s scroll — consideration — at Sir Reginald’s sword — courage — at Princess Poofington’s mist — hope — at Captain Cuddles’s map — the adventures they took together, usually as far as a picnic — at Lord Snugglepants’s lotus — the peace she wished for everyone and did not always keep. She named each dog as if they had been ministers all along. The courtiers beamed, discovering that their outlandish props had been promoted to allegory. The dogs received ear-scratches so vigorous they nearly achieved flight. Sebastian stayed behind the wood a moment longer, bewildered and, inconveniently, relieved.

“A masterpiece,” she said, clapping. “A true allegory of my reign.” Her eyes twinkled, then thinned. The hall’s laugh-echo died. “Sometimes one needs the kingdom to believe in an unbreakable strength, even when one feels a tremor. These visions fortify us.”

She did not ask him to scrape the canvas clean. That was the turn: not a speech about the market for magnificent lies, only her gloved finger leaving the sword where Barty had insisted it belong.

Sebastian stepped out. He set the sable brush down on the painted lotus, a small precise click, and let the afternoon finish the rest. A footman arrived with roast chicken in seven loyal portions. A purse arrived with enough pigment for years. The Queen’s face, under all the carnival, was still the face he had begun that morning, only now it was laughing. Through the tall windows the light had gone the colour of thin gold. The linseed smell seemed, briefly, like a kind of peace, and the clock in the next room, which had never stopped, sounded almost tactful.
characters: Sebastian Quill (royal portraitist), Queen Adelina (sitter with seven lapdogs)
